1.goal: To open the lesson on a situation she knows, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine at this point.
run: Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she follows a call with three people and comes into it to check one thing.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you listen to a call with three people. Then you come into the call and ask what you need.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of one call. What were they talking about?”
1.expected: One call from her own work, named in a sentence or two. A complete answer looks like “Last week, the planning call for the B2 group. Two coordinators disagreed about the tests and I did not say anything.” — the situation and the fact that she stayed quiet.
1.support: If nothing comes to mind, name two kinds of call and let her pick one: a planning call, or a call with a publisher or a supplier.
1.challenge: Ask what stopped her from speaking in that call.
1.monitoring: Whether the call she picks is one where she stayed quiet. That is the situation the lesson works on.
1.evidence: The call she names, in her words. It is worth coming back to at the close.
1.transition: Move on when she has named one concrete call.

2.goal: To establish who is in the call, what it is for, and what she needs to leave it with.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “I need to know whether the second reading text is staying, because my group starts in four weeks.” The brief gives it in the third line; what the three people disagree about is not on this screen, and the first listening is where it appears.
2.support: If she answers with what the call is about, point at “What you need” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask which of the three people she would find hardest to interrupt, and why.
2.monitoring: Whether she states what she needs from the brief or starts guessing the content of the call.
2.evidence: Whether she can say what she needs without rereading the brief.
2.transition: Move on when she has said what she needs to leave the call with.

3.goal: To have her commit to three guesses before she listens, so the first listening has something to confirm.
3.interaction: T–S, guessing out loud. Nothing is confirmed or corrected here.
run: Read the three questions with her.
Take one answer on each. Leave them unconfirmed: the call settles them.
Note her third answer — what would make her speak. It comes back on screen 9.
exact: Before moving on: “Those are your guesses. Now we listen and see.”
3.expected: There is no answer key on this screen: the three questions are open. For your reference, what the call will show: Peter and Rachel disagree about whether to cut the second reading text or move it; Marta, who chairs, summarizes and closes the item without taking a side; and nobody asks anything of the person who is only listening.
3.support: If she answers about meetings in general, ask her to answer about a call on one unit of a coursebook.
3.challenge: Ask what would have to be true for her to speak in the first two minutes of a call.
3.monitoring: Whether she risks a guess or waits to be told.
3.evidence: Her third answer, to compare with the stop where she comes in on screen 9.
3.transition: Move on when all three questions have an answer, right or wrong.

4.goal: To follow the whole call once for the general picture: who is there and what is at stake.
4.interaction: S listens alone, then T–S on the two questions.
run: Read the two questions with her before you press Play.
Play the call once, at Normal.
Take her answers, and then ask which of her guesses from screen 3 the call confirms. Keep the transcript for the next screen.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Listen once, all the way through. Find the answers to these two questions.”
4.expected: Three people — Marta, Peter and Rachel — in a planning call about one unit of the coursebook. Nobody decides anything: at the end Marta says “let us take it as a proposal, not a decision.”
4.support: If she lost track of who is who, play it once at Slower and ask only the first question.
4.challenge: Ask which of the three she thinks makes the decision in the end, before she hears it again.
4.monitoring: Whether she follows the whole call or stops at the first turn she does not catch. Two of the three voices are female, and telling them apart is part of the task.
4.evidence: How much of the call she followed in one listening without support.
4.transition: Move on when both questions have an answer, even a partial one.

5.goal: To attribute each thing that is said to the speaker who says it, and to go back to the line to prove it.
5.interaction: S listens and places the five alone, then T–S with the transcript.
run: Play the call again, and let her place all five. She presses Check when she has finished.
Then go through the five out loud. On each, open the transcript and ask her to find the line.
Spend the time that is left on the statement that nobody says.
exact: On each statement: “Who says that? Find the line.”
On the approval: “Rachel talks about approval. What does she actually say?”
5.expected: Peter: “Wants the second reading text taken out” (“I would drop the second reading text”). Rachel: “Wants it kept, in a different place” (“If the second text moved to the start of the unit…”) · “Says the students cannot read two sources against each other” (“that is the thing they actually cannot do yet”). Marta: “States no position of their own” — she gives turns, summarizes and closes the item. nobody says this: “Says the change has already been approved” — Rachel says “To get it approved? That I cannot tell you.” and Marta calls it “a proposal, not a decision.”
5.support: If one will not come, play only the turn it depends on, and ask who is speaking before asking what they want.
5.challenge: Ask which of the two positions is closer to what her own group needs.
5.monitoring: Whether she places Marta as someone who agrees. Marta never states a position; if she does this, go back to the line where Marta summarizes the disagreement.
5.evidence: Whether she could point at a line for each answer, or answered from impression.
5.transition: Move on when the five are placed and the approval has been discussed.

6.goal: To have her notice that a turn in a call can do something other than state a position.
6.interaction: S alone on the activity, then T–S.
run: Let her classify the six lines and press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each, ask who says it and what would change in the call without it.
Leave the discussion of the line that moved the call for the next screen.
6.expected: stating a position: “Unit seven is too long for the hours we have.” (Peter) · “It is the only place where they read two sources against each other.” (Rachel). putting a proposal: “If the second text moved to the start of the unit…” (Rachel). reformulating someone else: “So we agree the unit is too long. We disagree about which part goes.” (Marta) · “I am not sure we agree it is too long.” (Rachel, reframing Marta's summary). conceding: “That is a different proposal, and it is a better one than mine, honestly.” (Peter).
6.support: On each line, ask: is the speaker saying what they want, or doing something with what someone else said?
6.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the positions into a reformulation of it.
6.monitoring: Whether she places Rachel's “I am not sure we agree it is too long.” as a position. It sounds like disagreement, and it works on Marta's summary.
6.evidence: Which line she places as reformulating, and in what words she explains it.
6.transition: Move on when the six are sorted.

7.goal: To have her explain how one line changed the direction of the call, and hear the language that does it.
run: Read the question and the two lines on screen with her.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open the reveal and read it with her. Then ask her for one sentence that refuses a summary, about a meeting of her own.
exact: If she does not see it: “What was the call about before Rachel spoke? And after?”
Asking for an example: “Someone says: so we all agree the course is too expensive. You do not agree. What do you say?”
7.expected: Before the line, the call was about which part to cut; after it, about the order of the unit. Rachel does not say no to Peter: she does not accept Marta's summary, “So we agree the unit is too long.” From the reveal: “I am not sure we agree that…” refuses the summary; “It is too long the way it is sequenced.” accepts the fact and changes the cause; “That is a different proposal.” says what just happened before answering it.
7.support: Play Rachel's turn once more, and ask what word she changes in Marta's sentence.
7.challenge: Ask what Peter could have said to keep the call on his proposal.
7.monitoring: Whether she finds the change before the reveal, and whether her own example refuses the summary without contradicting the person.
7.evidence: Her example sentence, in her words.
7.transition: Move on when the reveal has been read and she has given one example.

8.goal: To practice coming into a call: say what she heard first, then ask one thing.
8.interaction: T–S, spoken. You say a line from the call; she comes in.
run: Play the five sentences once, and ask her which part names what was heard and which part asks.
Say the three lines below, one at a time, as if you were in the call. After each one she comes in.
When she starts with her own subject, ask her to start again with what she heard.
exact: Line 1: “Unit seven is too long for the hours we have.”
Line 2: “If the second text moved to the start of the unit, it would have the whole unit behind it.”
Line 3: “Then let us take it as a proposal, not a decision.”
Rebuilding an opening: “Start again, and say first what you heard.”
8.expected: Three turns that name something said before asking. For example, after line 1: “Sorry to jump in — I heard you say the unit is too long. Which part would go?”; after line 2: “Can I check one thing? If the text moves, does the plan document change too?”; after line 3: “Just to be clear, so nothing is decided yet?”. Any opening anchored in the line is correct, including forms that are not on the screen.
8.support: If the opening does not come, say the first three words — “I heard you…” — and let her finish.
8.challenge: Ask for the same turn with a different opening each time.
8.monitoring: Whether what she heard comes before the question, or after it as a justification.
8.evidence: How many of the three turns started with what she heard, without help.
8.transition: Move on when she has come in after the three lines.

9.goal: To come into the recorded call at a moment she chooses, ask the one thing she needs, and hand the call back.
9.interaction: Role-play over the recording. You answer as Marta when she comes in.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose one.
Play Part One, Two and Three in order. After each part, wait: the silence is her decision.
When she comes in, answer as Marta, and once ask back one of the two questions below.
The sentence starters stay closed. Open them only if she stops, and close them again. Leave corrections for screen 11.
exact: Asking back for precision: “Sorry, are you asking about the text, or about the hours?”
Asking back for a position: “And which of the two would you go with?”
9.expected: One turn at a stop she chose, with the four things on the list: an opening that names something said (for option A, for example “I heard Peter say the second text might go.”; for option B, “I heard Rachel say the new order would change the plan.”), the one question she needs (A: whether the text is staying; B: whether the new order is decided and who approves it), why it matters to her in one sentence, and the call handed back (“That was all I needed. Sorry, you were saying?”). She also answers your question back.
9.support: If she lets all three stops pass, play Part Two again and point at the first item on the list.
9.challenge: If she comes in at the first stop, play on to the third and ask for a second turn that does not repeat the first.
9.monitoring: At which stop she comes in, and what her first words are.
9.evidence: The option she chose, the stop where she came in, and her first sentence written word for word. It goes into the boards on screen 11.
9.transition: Move on when she has come in at least once and handed the call back.

10.goal: To keep the conversation going after her turn in the call: answer two questions from Marta with a reason, and ask one back.
10.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are Marta, talking to her after the call.
run: Ask the two questions below, one at a time.
After each answer, wait. The reason usually comes after a pause.
Then ask her to put one question to you about what happens next, and answer it.
exact: Question 1: “You asked about the second text. For your group, is it better to cut it or to move it?”
Question 2: “If the new order is approved, what would you need from us before your group starts?”
Handing the turn over: “Anything else you need from me?”
10.expected: Two answers, each with a reason, and one question from her. The call does not decide the first question, so any choice with a reason is correct — a complete answer looks like “I would move it. My group needs that reading, and they would have the whole unit to prepare for it.” On the second, something concrete she needs: the new plan, a date, who approves it. Her question can be as small as “When will we know if it is approved?”.
10.support: If she answers without a reason, ask “Why that one?” and wait.
10.challenge: Disagree once: “Peter thinks half of them do not finish it anyway.” Let her answer him.
10.monitoring: Whether the reason comes in the same turn as the answer, and whether her question comes without you asking for it.
10.evidence: Whether she gave reasons without being asked, and whether she asked a question of her own.
10.transition: Move on when she has answered the two questions and asked one.

11.goal: To give one piece of feedback she can use, and to come into the call again under a harder condition.
11.interaction: T–S, filling the boards together, then the replay.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve in the boards on screen.
Write the first sentence of her turn on screen 9 as she said it, and build a clearer version with her in the fourth box.
Open the replay. Play the part before the stop where she waited longest, and when she comes in, answer as Peter, who wants the text out.
exact: Answering as Peter: “Honestly, I would drop that text. Half of them do not finish it.”
11.expected: The same turn at a new stop, with the point to improve used: an opening that names what was said, her question kept after Peter disagrees, and the call handed back. A complete second version sounds like “I hear you, Peter. What I still need to know is whether it is decided. My group starts in four weeks.”
11.support: Point at the line on screen and let her use it word for word the first time.
11.challenge: Answer as Peter once more, and let her hand the call back to Marta.
11.monitoring: Whether she keeps her question when the answer is a disagreement.
11.evidence: Whether the point to improve from the boards appeared in the replay.
11.transition: Move on when the replay has been said.

12.goal: To close on what was worked on, let her say how confident she feels, and leave the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “In your next call, come in once to check one thing. Start with what you heard.”
12.expected: The recap has seven lines, and all seven were done if the lesson ran to the end: following three voices and keeping track of who said what, telling a position from a proposal, hearing when someone changes the direction of the call, coming in to check one point, naming what she heard before asking, handing the call back, and answering questions after the call with a reason. The confidence scale is hers, and it may come out lower than what you saw.
12.support: If she marks everything low, name the stop where she came in and her first sentence.
12.challenge: Ask when her next call like this one is, and which phrase she would take into it.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed. The gap is worth noting.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and anything she said about the pre-class.
12.transition: End here. The next lesson is about describing a class she watched.
